newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Deng death likely to delay energy decisions.
newsitem.headline: Deng death likely to delay energy decisions.

text.p: Foreign companies remain eager to invest in China's growing energy sector despite the death of Deng Xiaoping and even though it is likely to slow an already cumbersome approval process, analysts said on Thursday.

Key decisions on projects are likely to be delayed while the political leadership is decided, although that will present few worries for oil companies used to long delays in decision making and at times an unpredictable oil policy, they said.
"The process in China for approving large foreign joint venture projects is already slow," said Kang Wu, a fellow at Hawaii's East-West Center.

"But if the Chinese leadership is eager to prove to the world there are no problems with the transition they might want to approve proposals to show nothing is unusual," he said. China announced Deng's death late on Wednesday, marking the end of an 18-year rule that transformed China from a backward Stalinist state into an economic power that is an increasingly large net importer of crude oil and products.
Its refinery sector has a production capacity of 4.3 million barrels per day (bpd) but utilisation suggests actual production is more like 3.0 to 3.2 million bpd, analysts said.
In recent years, China has slowly been opening the door to foreign investment to help exploit oil reserves and improve the efficiency of its refining industry.

Several billion dollars in investments are at stake with companies seeking a stepping stone into China, cautious of volatile policies but swayed by rapid growth and a market of 1.2 billion people nowhere else can match.
Deng's failing health in recent years and his move to a figurehead rather than an active policy maker has allowed most companies to factor in his eventual loss.

"China's political system has already been in transition to (President) Jiang Zemin, therefore it seems unlikely there will be change in the country's political situation," a Japan National Oil Corp spokesman said.

David Fridely, a researcher on the energy analysis programme of the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in the United States, said China had already invested heavily in its economic growth and history suggested there would be few financial problems.
"There is no indication that those in power have any different kind of orientation in terms of faster or slower liberalisation than what has been set in motion," he said.
"Even during the worse turmoil of the cultural revolution, China never stopped grain import programme and never stopped payments of foreign debts," he said.
"Virtually every major actor in China has inevitably a large stake in the success of economic growth," Fridley said.

But certain key decisions face delay as China goes through the transition of leadership following Deng's death. And that process could take a long time, possibly beyond the Communist Party Congress in later in the year, the analysts said.

Chinese National Offshore Oil Corp, a partner with Royal Dutch/Shell was hopeful last week it would gain approval in the first half of the year to build a 600,000 tonnes-per-year petrochemical complex.
Yukong Ltd also expected its 100,000 bpd export refinery would soon gain approval. Giant Saudi Aramco is trying to get approval with Sinochem for a 200,000 bpd refinery.
Various oil majors, including Exxon Corp and Chevron Corp are involved in energy projects, including exploration and production.

"These companies have put a lot of money into China already," said one analyst who asked not to be identified. "They would not have done so if they thought there could be problems when he (Deng) died."
Japanese firms have also been active in China and Kazuya Fujime, head of Tokyo's Institute of Energy Economics think tank, said a cautious period was ahead.
"They will not react favorably even to the slightest hint of a return to conservative policies," Fujime said.
